region.zh: 廣寒樓，南原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story set in a magistrate's tenure in Namwon (Cholla); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Honest Witch', eBook #51002

summary.en: Song Sang-in, who hates witches as deceivers of the people, becomes magistrate of Namwon and orders any witch found there beaten to death. Resting at Kwang-han Pavilion he sees a woman ride up with a witch's drum on her head — a mutang who stayed knowing the order. 'There are true mutangs and false mutangs,' she says; false ones ought to be killed, but not an honest one. Put to the proof, she prepares food and wine, dons the magistrate's clothes, shakes the spirit-bell and calls up his dead friend, recounting their school days, examination struggles, official experiences and secrets only the two of them knew — not a single mistake. The magistrate weeps, recalls his order, and gives her rich rewards.
summary.zh: 宋尚運疾巫如仇，蒞任南原即下令殺巫。遊廣寒樓，見一婦頂巫鼓騎馬而來。自稱真巫，願以身試。乃設祭衣冠搖鈴召魂，所述死者與令之同窗、科場、宦遊、密語，無一不合。令泣曰：『巫果有真偽也。』遂罷前令，厚賞遣之。

sensitivity.note: Depicts the Korean kut and mutang (shamaness) tradition from a Confucian magistrate's view; recorded as historical belief.

passages.text: Song Sang-in's mind was upright and his spirit true. He hated witches with all his might, and regarded them as deceivers of the people. 'By their so-called prayers,' said he, 'they devour the people's goods.' When he was appointed magistrate of Namwon County he issued the order: 'If any witch is found in this county, let her be beaten to death.' The whole place was so thoroughly spied upon that all the witches made their escape to other prefectures.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Honest Witch' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day resting at Kwang-han Pavilion he saw a woman approaching on horseback with a witch's drum on her head — a mutang. Asked why she had not fled, she replied, 'There are true mutangs and false mutangs. False mutangs ought to be killed, but you would not kill an honest mutang, would you? I am an honest mutang; I knew you would not kill me, so I remained here in peace.' 'Let's put the matter to the test and see. If I am not proven honest, let me die.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Honest Witch' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The mutang spread her mat in the courtyard, placed food and wine in order, donned a suit of the magistrate's clothes, lifted her eyes toward heaven, uttered the strange magic sounds by which spirits are called, and shook a tinkling bell. In a little she turned and said, 'I've come' — and told the sad story of his dead friend's sickness and death, of their days at school, their examination difficulties, their experiences in office, and secrets that only they two knew, not a single mistake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Honest Witch' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The magistrate began to cry: 'The soul of my friend is really present; I can no longer doubt or deny it. Alas! I thought mutangs were a brood of liars, but now I know that there are true mutangs as well as false.' He gave her rich rewards, sent her away in safety, recalled his order against witches, and refrained from any matters pertaining to them for ever after.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Honest Witch' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: After the Rains the Mountains Weep

region.zh: 漢京成均館（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of the reign of King Se-jong (r. 1418-1450); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Whom the King Honours', eBook #51002

summary.en: At the Spring Festival picnic of the Confucian College, one raw countryman stays behind alone to guard the sacred precincts of the temple. King Se-jong's eunuch reports it; the King sends for him, asks why he remains, and tests him with half a verse — 'After the rains the mountains weep' — which the student completes: 'Before the wind the grass is tipsy.' Delighted, the King makes him a special graduate on the spot, gives him the red coat, a horse and flute-players, and sends him to show himself at the picnic, where his classmates break up in consternation. He became later, through the King's favour, a great and noted man.
summary.zh: 世宗時成均館諸生春遊，一鄉曲書生獨留守廟中。王聞之召見，試以半句云『雨後山如泣』，生應聲對曰『風前草欲傾』。王大悅，即賜進士及第，花帽紅袍，鼓吹遊街。諸生駭散。後官至顯要。

passages.text: Students of the Confucian College were having a picnic to celebrate the Spring Festival. One student from the country, of no account to others, thought that while the rest went away to enjoy themselves some one ought to stay behind to guard the sacred precincts of the temple, so he decided to forgo the pleasures of the picnic, stay behind and watch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Whom the King Honours' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The King sent a eunuch to see how many students had remained on guard. All had gone off on the picnic except one raw countryman in sole charge. His Majesty sent for him and asked, 'When all have gone off for a gay time, why is it that you remain alone?' He replied, 'To leave the sacred temple wholly deserted did not seem to me right, so I stayed.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Whom the King Honours' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Do you know how to write verses?' asked the King, and gave him one-half of a verse: 'After the rains the mountains weep.' At once the student replied, 'Before the wind the grass is tipsy.' The King, delighted, made him a special graduate on the spot, gave him his diploma and flowers for his hat, ordered for him the red coat, a horse to ride on and flute-players, and said, 'Go now to the picnic-party and show yourself.' The company, in consternation and surprise, broke up and returned home at once; and this special graduate became later, through the favour of the King, a great and noted man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Whom the King Honours' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The King Reads the Book of Changes by Moonlight

texts.period: Story of the reign of King Se-jong (r. 1418-1450); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Fortunes of Yoo', eBook #51002

summary.en: Yoo, a friendless petty official about to quit Seoul, is smuggled into the Palace for the night and, wandering over a broken wall in the rainy-season moonlight, meets a strolling gentleman with a staff: it is King Se-jong himself. Called in to sit on a mat beside him, Yoo explains the character by character the passage of the Book of Changes that has given the King special difficulty, and they read together all through the night. 'You have all this knowledge and yet have never been made use of? Alas, for my country!' Over the following days the King promotes him one degree at a time, weathering each protest of the ministers, until at a banquet he opens the book before them all and not one of the highest ministers can answer: 'Any one who understands it surely ought to be promoted.' Yoo becomes royal teacher of the Changes and Head of the Confucian College.
summary.zh: 柳某官微將歸鄉，夜入禁苑，遇曳杖散步之人，乃世宗也。坐而共讀《易》，至難解處，柳逐字為訓，通宵不倦。王歎曰：『有才如此而不用，國之憾也！』其後日進一階，群臣屢諫不納。宴集時王出《易》詰群臣，無一人能對。遂命為侍講，官至大司成。

passages.text: There was a man of Yong-nam, named Yoo, who lived in the days of Se-jong, a countryman who had no friends and no influence. Disheartened, he decided to leave the city and go back to his country home. A palace secretary who knew him offered to let him sleep the night in the royal office to see the Palace, but the secretary failed to come; the gates were shut, and Yoo was a prisoner for the night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Fortunes of Yoo' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The night was beautifully clear. It was the time of the rainy season, and a portion of the wall had fallen from the enclosure in front. So Yoo climbed over the broken wall, and found himself in a beautiful park with trees, lakes and walks. Suddenly a man appeared with a nice new cap on his head, carrying a staff, walking slowly toward him with a servant — no other than King Se-jong, taking a stroll in the moonlight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Fortunes of Yoo' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I am the master of this house,' said the King, and made him sit down on a mat beside him. Learning how Yoo had passed special examinations in the classics yet remained unpromoted, he asked whether he knew the Book of Changes; then he ordered a eunuch to bring it, opened the part that had given him special difficulty, and the stranger explained it character by character with convincing clearness, so that they read together all through the night. When they separated the King sighed, 'You have all this knowledge and yet have never been made use of? Alas, for my country!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Fortunes of Yoo' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Day after day the King appointed him to higher office, one degree at a time, and the officials protested each time, so much so that his Majesty seemed to yield — and promoted him higher still. At a royal banquet the high Ministers said quietly that it was not fitting for so obscure a person to hold so important an office. The King made no reply, but ordered the Book of Changes, opened it at the place of special difficulty and inquired its meaning; even among the highest ministers not one could give an answer. 'Any one who understands it surely ought to be promoted. You, all of you, fail to grasp its meaning, while Yoo has explained it all to me. I shall promote him still more and more, so cease from all opposition.' Yoo became royal teacher of the Choo-yuk and rose to Head of the Confucian College, first in influence, surpassing all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Fortunes of Yoo' (1913); not verbatim.

region.zh: 漢京革帶坊（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story told by Captain Choi Won-so in prison (year Pyong-sin); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'An Encounter with a Hobgoblin', eBook #51002

summary.en: Young Choi Won-so takes a vacant house in Belt Town. Night after night a beautiful woman enters his room and retreats backwards out of the gate, eluding his grasp. Then one night a curtain drops from the ceiling, a great fire of coals descends before him, the room seems all on fire — and at the first cock-crow all is gone. The following night a great stout man in a soldier's felt hat drags him from the room, swings him round, flings him into the air to fall in Chulla province, and tosses him up three times more, while a dozen people behind the garden wall cry 'Don't hurt him' — till one of them leads his tormentor away. Choi lies senseless till morning and the family leaves the haunted house, never to go back.
summary.zh: 崔元洙少年僦居漢京革帶坊凶宅。夜夜有美人入室，倒退出門，追之不及。一夕屋中垂簾降火，烈焰繞身，雞鳴始滅。次日有偉夫戴軍帽者入室，拽其人出，拋擲空中，飛越三道而墜於全羅，如是者三；牆內十餘人齊呼『勿傷之』，然無如之何。昏暈至旦，舉家遷避，不復居焉。

passages.text: When I was young I met with a hobgoblin which, by the fraction of a hair, almost cost me my life. Hearing of a vacant place in Belt Town I made application and got it; my father and the family occupied the inner quarters while I lived in the front room. One night, late, when I was half asleep, the door suddenly opened, and a woman came in and stood just before the lamp — a beauty I had seen before at a scholar friend's home. I arose to take her by the hand, but she began walking backwards, eluding me till she passed out at the gate and disappeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'An Encounter with a Hobgoblin' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the next night she came again and stood before the lamp, and again retreated backward out of the gate. A few nights later, a sound of crackling paper came from above the ceiling; a curtain was let down dividing the room in two; then a large fire of coals descended right in front of me, and an immense heat filled the place, as though all were on fire with no way of escape. At the first cock-crow the noise ceased, the curtain went up, the fire was gone, and the place was as though swept with a broom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'An Encounter with a Hobgoblin' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The following night a great stout man suddenly opened the door — a soldier's felt hat, a blue tunic like a yamen underling. He took hold of me and dragged me out; young and vigorous, I entered on a tussle and lost. He swung me round, carried me up to the highest terrace and threw me down; then took me by the two hands and flung me up into the air, till I went half-way and more to heaven. In my fall I went shooting past Kyong-keui Province, past Choong-chong, and at last fell to the ground in Chulla, seeing all the county towns of the three provinces as clear as day. He tossed me up again and again, two or three times in all, while within the garden wall a dozen people in military hats and coats kept shouting, 'Don't hurt him, don't hurt him. The man is a gentleman of the military class' — till one of the group came forward, took my tormentor by the hand and led him away. I lay motionless at the foot of the terrace till the following morning, and we all left the haunted house, never to go back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'An Encounter with a Hobgoblin' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Snake Who Was Born as a Son

region.en: Water Gate, Seoul city wall (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Ancient-days tale collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Snake's Revenge', eBook #51002

summary.en: A valiant archer living near the Water Gate of Seoul sees a great snake held fast between the iron pickets — head through, body stuck — shoots it in the head, pounds it to a pulp and leaves it. Soon his wife bears a son who from the first fears and hates his father. Lying awake one noon behind his sleeve, the officer sees the boy glare at him, fetch a knife and strike; he seizes the knife and kills the boy with a club. The mother lifting the quilt finds not her child but a huge coiled snake, and on its head the scar-mark of the arrow. The father reasons with it — you had your revenge and have returned to your original shape; let us drop the past — and the snake, bowing its head, departs through the Water Gate between the bars and does not appear again.
summary.zh: 水門畔有勇士，見巨蛇首過鐵柵而身不得出，射殺之，搗為泥。未幾妻產子，子自幼畏父、恨父。一日晝寢佯寐，子窺之，持刀刺之，父覺，奪刀擊殺之。母舉衾視之，兒已化巨蟒，首有箭瘢。父語之曰：『爾既報復，復歸本形，前事可置。』蛇俯首聽命，自穿水門鐵柵而去，不復見。

sensitivity.note: Reincarnation-revenge tale; Buddhist transmigration doctrine in folk form.

passages.text: There lived in ancient days an archer whose home was near the Water Gate of Seoul, a man of great strength and famous for his valour. A great snake was seen making its way by the Water Gate, its head already passed between the iron bars but its body held fast. The soldier drew an arrow and shot the snake in the head; then he drew it out, pounded it into a pulp, and left it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Snake's Revenge' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: A little time later the man's wife conceived and bore a son. From the first the child was afraid of its father, and as it grew it hated the sight of him more and more, while the father grew to dislike him. On a certain day, when there were just the two of them in the room, the officer lay down for a siesta covering his face with his sleeve, but keeping his eye on the boy. The child glared at his father, and thinking him asleep, got a knife and made a thrust at him. The man jumped, grabbed the knife, and with a club gave the boy a blow that left him dead on the spot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Snake's Revenge' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The mother, in tears, covered the little form with a quilt for burial; in a little the quilt began to move, and beneath it the child was gone and there lay coiled a huge snake instead, with on its head the scar mark of the arrow that he had shot. The father said to the snake, 'Your intention to take revenge through becoming my son was a horrible deed. You have already had your revenge, and have once more transmigrated into your original shape; let us drop the past and be friends from now on.' The snake with bowed head seemed to listen intently; then the father opened the door, and the snake departed, making straight for the Water Gate, passed out between the bars, and did not again appear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Snake's Revenge' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fog-Bound Giant of the Cursed County

region.en: North Ham-kyong province county seat (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 咸鏡北道邑治（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Olden-times tale collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Brave Magistrate', eBook #51002

summary.en: In a county of North Ham-kyong an evil-smelling goblin destroys every magistrate within ten days of arrival; a hundred men refuse the post until a brave, friendless soldier accepts. Arming himself with a long knife, he notes the fishy stench that enters like a mist by the outer gate. On the appointed day, fortified by whisky, he sees a thing come wrapped in fog, three or four embraces in waist size and fifteen feet high, headless, with only two dreadful eyes rolling on top. He rushes at it with a great shout and strikes it with his sword: the sound of thunder, and the whole thing dissipates, the foul smell vanishing at once. Thought dead by his retainers, he comes to life and looks at them in anger; from that time on there is no more smell.
summary.zh: 咸鏡北道某邑有妖，屆任者旬日必死，百人辭而不就。有一勇卒慨然受之。至期縱飲仗劍。果見怪物裹霧入門，腰可三四抱，高約丈五，無首無臂，惟頂上二目如電。公大喝一劍揮之，聲如雷震，怪散而腥風頓息。僚屬以為已死，方聚而哭之，公霍然而起，眾駭然。自是邑中無妖。

passages.text: In olden times in one of the counties of North Ham-kyong Province there was an evil-smelling goblin that caused great destruction to life. Successive magistrates died in great agony within ten days or so of arrival, so that a hundred or more were asked to take the post and all refused. At last one brave soldier, without any influence socially or politically, accepted: 'Even though there is a devil there, all men will not die, surely. I shall make a trial of him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Brave Magistrate' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: He found himself alone in the yamen, all others having taken flight, and constantly carried a long knife at his belt, for he noticed from the first day a fishy, stinking odour that seemed to make its entry by the outer gate wrapped in mist, growing daily more marked. When the time arrived for him to die, the yamen-runners and servants again ran away. He kept a jar of whisky by his side and drank frequently to fortify his soul, and on this day grew very drunk and waited.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Brave Magistrate' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last he saw something coming through the main gateway wrapped in fog, three or four embraces in waist size and fifteen feet or so high. There was no head to it, nor were body or arms visible; only on the top were two dreadful eyes rolling wildly. The magistrate jumped up, rushed toward it, gave a great shout and struck it with his sword: there was the sound of thunder, and the whole thing dissipated, the foul smell disappearing at once. The retainers, thinking him dead, gathered to prepare his burial; they raised him up when suddenly he came to life, looked at them in anger, and asked what they meant. From that time on there was no more smell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Brave Magistrate' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The God of War Sends a Messenger about His Temple

region.en: Temple site, south of Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城南關帝廟（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of the Japanese War era (1592-1598); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Temple to the God of War', eBook #51002

summary.en: During the Japanese War the Ming general tells the Korean king that the victory was due to the help of Kwan, the God of War, and temples must be built in gratitude — one south and one east of the city. The site conference deadlocks, with Yi Hang-bok in charge. One day a great strapping military officer calls at Yi's house, sends the retainers out, delivers his message and leaves: he was a messenger of the God of War, come to show where the temple ought to be. 'It is not a matter for time only, but for the eternities to come. If we do not get it right the God of War will find no peace.' Yi used all his efforts, and at last the building was placed on the approved site, where it now stands.
summary.zh: 壬辰倭亂，明將言勝倭者關帝之力也，宜建廟以報。南北二廟議基不決，李好閔主其事。一日有偉丈夫武人來謁，屏左右密語而去。李告友曰：『此關帝之使也，來示廟基。此地非一時之計，乃萬世之計；基不正則帝不安。』遂如其言定基，廟至今存焉。

sensitivity.note: Kwan (Guan Yu) cult introduced via the Ming army during the Imjin War; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: During the Japanese War in the reign of Son-jo, the Mings sent a great army that came east, drove out the enemy and restored peace. The general of the Mings informed his Korean Majesty that the victory was due to the help of Kwan, the God of War: 'This being the case, you ought not to continue without temples in which to express your gratitude to him.' So they built him houses of worship, one to the south and one to the east of the city.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Temple to the God of War' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: In examining the sites they could not agree on the one to the south; an official called Yi Hang-bok was in charge of the conference. One day when Yi was at home a military officer called and wished to see him — a great strapping fellow, splendidly built. He asked that all Yi's retainers be sent out till he talked to him privately; after finishing his message he said good-bye and left.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Temple to the God of War' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yi told his old friend that a very extraordinary thing had happened: the military man was none other than a messenger of the God of War, come on account of their not yet having decided the site for the Temple. 'He came to show me where it ought to be. He urged that it was not a matter for time only, but for the eternities to come. If we do not get it right the God of War will find no peace.' Yi used all his efforts, and at last the building was placed on the approved site, where it now stands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Temple to the God of War' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mother's Ghost Who Loved the Kut

texts.period: Olden-days tale; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'A Visit from the Shades', eBook #51002

summary.en: Dressing for office, a Palace secretary dozes and dreams he meets his dead mother on foot on East Palace Street. 'I have already left the world,' she says, 'and I am going to partake of the sacrifice at the witches' prayer service our servant is holding at Yong-san.' But why not to her son's own house, with its four seasonal sacrificial days? 'Your sacrifices are of no interest to me; I like the prayers of the witches. If there is no medium we spirits find no satisfaction.' Waking, the secretary sends for the servant — who reports that at the Yong-san kut the possessed mutang called him by name, 'This is a servant from our house,' and gave him drink, saying she had met her son going to the Palace on her way. The secretary calls the mutang, makes a great offering on behalf of his mother's spirit, and ever after sacrifices to her four times a year.
summary.zh: 某相公晨起盥沐，假寐夢亡母步行於宮門外。問之，曰：『吾已去世，今赴龍山奴婢家巫祭。』曰：『家有四時之祭，何不歸享？』母曰：『爾家之祭吾不樂；吾好巫覡之禱。無憑依者，鬼神不得安也。』醒而遣僕視之，僕言巫方降神，自稱乃主人之母，且賜酒曰『吾適遇吾子入宮也』。相公大慟，延巫盛祭，後四時致祭不輟。

sensitivity.note: Ancestor-spirit and kut ritual; record documents belief, not prescription.

passages.text: There was a minister in olden days who, once when he was Palace Secretary, was getting ready for office in the morning. Sleep overcame him, and in the dream he was mounted and on his journey, crossing the bridge at the entrance to East Palace Street, when suddenly he saw his mother coming toward him on foot. 'Why do you come thus, mother, not in a chair, but on foot?' She replied, 'I have already left the world, and things are not where I am as they are where you are, and so I walk.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'A Visit from the Shades' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'We have a servant living at Yong-san, and they are having a witches' prayer service there just now, so I am going to partake of the sacrifice,' said the mother. The secretary asked why she did not go to his own home with its four seasons of sacrificial days, and she replied, 'Your sacrifices are of no interest to me, I like the prayers of the witches. If there is no medium we spirits find no satisfaction. I am in a hurry and cannot wait longer' — and she was gone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'A Visit from the Shades' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The secretary sent a servant to Yong-san, who returned with the news: at the koot the mutang had said the spirit that possessed her was the mother of the master; on his appearance she called out his name — 'This is a servant from our house' — gave him a big glass of spirit, and added, 'On my way here I met my son going into the Palace.' Overhearing this, the secretary broke down and cried. He called the mutang, made her a great offering on behalf of his mother's spirit, and ever afterwards sacrificed to her four times a year at each returning season.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'A Visit from the Shades' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Three Devils Sit in a Row before the Captain

region.zh: 咸鏡北道官舍（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of Captain Yee Man-ji (c. 1600s); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Fearless Captain', eBook #51002

summary.en: Yee Man-ji, brave as a lion, sits undisturbed on his verandah while a ball of fire bounces through his house in a thunderstorm; that year his whole family sickens and dies. Settling in North Ham-kyong where all his predecessors died of goblin influence, he repairs the dreaded official quarters. One night three objects like tree-stumps wrapped in black sackcloth come jumping in and sit before him, closer and closer, till he is backed against the wall. 'Who are you, anyhow? If you have any complaint, say so, and I'll see to it.' 'I'm hungry,' says the middle devil. 'Hungry, are you? Move back and I'll have food prepared in abundance' — then, repeating a magic formula, he snaps his fingers and strikes at the first devil with his fist, cutting his hand on the floor. 'We'll go, we'll go, since you treat guests thus,' they shout, and bundle out; he has oxen killed and a sacrifice offered, and they return no more.
summary.zh: 李萬枝膽氣過人。雷火滾宅，端坐不動，而闔家當歲疫死。後官咸鏡北道，入居厲壇之舍。夜有三物如裹黑布之樹樁，跳而前，列坐於公案之側，愈逼愈近。公喝曰：『有冤則言，吾為汝理。』中鬼曰：『餓，餓，餓。』公曰：『退而待，吾將大饗汝。』乃誦咒彈指擊之，手破血流。三鬼呼曰『既如此待客，吾去矣』，踉蹌而遁。翌日屠牛設祭，怪遂絕。

passages.text: There was formerly a soldier, Yee Man-ji of Yong-nam, a strong and muscular fellow, brave as a lion, with green eyes and a terrible countenance, who frequently said, 'Fear! What is fear?' A sudden storm of rain came on with flashes of lightning, and a great ball of fire came tumbling into his home, rolling over the verandah, through the rooms, into the kitchen and out into the yard, bouncing about again and again. Yee sat in the outer verandah wholly undisturbed: 'I have done no wrong, therefore why need I fear the lightning?' During that year his family all fell ill and died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Fearless Captain' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yee came to Seoul, became a Captain of the Right Guard, and went to North Ham-kyong Province, where all his predecessors had died of goblin influences. Determined to live down all fear, he repaired the old quarters. One night, alone in the public office with a light burning, in the second watch a strange-looking object came out of the inner quarters, like the stump of a tree wrapped in black sackcloth, jumping along; two more followed, and the three sat in a row before him, coming closer and closer till he backed against the wall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Fearless Captain' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Who are you, anyhow; what kind of devil, pray, that you dare to push toward me so in my office? If you have any complaint or matter to set right, say so, and I'll see to it.' The middle devil said in reply, 'I'm hungry, I'm hungry, I'm hungry.' 'Hungry, are you? Very well, now just move back and I'll have food prepared for you in abundance.' He repeated a magic formula he had learned and snapped his fingers; the three devils seemed afraid. He closed his fist and struck a blow at the first devil, which dodged deftly; he hit the floor a sounding blow that cut his hand. Then they all shouted, 'We'll go, we'll go, since you treat guests thus,' and bundled out of the room. The following day he had oxen killed and a sacrifice offered to these devils, and they returned no more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Fearless Captain' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The King of Hades Wants a New Coat

region.en: Walls of the lower hell; Hai-ju (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Story of the afterlife of Pak Oo, Mayor of Hai-ju (c. 1600s); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The King of Yom-na (Hell)', eBook #51002

summary.en: A literary graduate of Yon-nan County falls ill; spirit soldiers bind him with a chain and lead him many hundreds of miles to a walled city with a structure whose height reaches to heaven, and lay him on his face before a most terrible king on a throne. Wrongly arrested — another man bears his name — he is released, but the King asks him to carry a message: his outer coat is worn to shreds; have his people send a new one, offered by fire at sacrifice. Asked for proof, the King of Hades reveals the secret of a broken head button hidden in the third volume of the Book of History. The scholar wakes — he has been dead three days — finds the Pak family in Seoul, is thrown out as a madman, then gives the button proof exactly; the family searches the Book of History, finds the missing button, and all enter upon mourning. They make the coat, offer it by fire, and three days after the sacrifice the scholar and the whole family dream that the King of Hades has come to give thanks.
summary.zh: 黃海道某進士暴卒，冥卒縛之，行數百里至冥府，見閻羅王坐殿。誤拘同名，釋之。王託以家書：外袍敝甚，乞家中焚寄新衣。進士索信物，王曰：『我生前有一朝珠缺角，藏《書經》第三卷中，人莫知之。』既甦，三日始活。詣漢京朴氏，其子怒而逐之；進士出朝珠為證，朴氏檢書果然，闔家舉哀。製衣焚祭，三日後舉家同夢，王來致謝。

sensitivity.note: Korean underworld (Yom-na/Yama) vision; parallels descent-to-underworld and Nekyia clusters.

passages.text: In Yon-nan County, Whang-hai Province, there was a certain literary graduate who fell ill one day. Suddenly several spirit soldiers appeared to him, saying, 'The Governor of the lower hell has ordered your arrest'; they bound him with a chain about his neck and led him away. They journeyed many hundreds of miles and reached a place with a very high wall, within which stood a great structure whose height reached to heaven. They entered the inner courtyard and laid him down on his face.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The King of Yom-na (Hell)' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Glancing up he saw what looked like a king seated on a throne, most terrible, grouped about with attendant officers, secretaries and soldiers. The King asked his name, age and calling, and the scholar answered that all his life he had heard that if you say your beads with love and pity in your heart you will escape hell, and so had given his time to calling on the Buddha and dispensing alms. A secretary returned with a message: 'You are not the person intended; it happens that you bear the same name, and you have thus been wrongly arrested. You may go now.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The King of Yom-na (Hell)' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The King sent him a commission: 'My outer coat I wear is worn to shreds. Ask my people to send me a new outer coat; prepare a sacrifice, offer the coat by fire, and it will reach me.' Asked how the family could be made to believe, the King said, 'When I was on earth one of my head buttons had a broken edge, and I hid it in the third volume of the Book of History. I alone know of it. If you give this as a proof they will listen.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The King of Yom-na (Hell)' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two soldier guards pushed him into a river as they left, and he awoke with a start to find he had been dead for three days. In Seoul he sought out the house of Pak Oo and told his story; the two graduate sons grew angry and ordered him pitched out, till he gave the story of the head button with great exactness. The book was taken down and examined, and sure enough in Vol. III of the Book of History was the button, which they had missed after their father's death. They entered upon mourning, made the outer coat, and offered it by fire before the ancestral altar; three days after the sacrifice the scholar dreamed, and the family of Pak dreamed too, that the King of Hades had come and given thanks for the coat. The guards had told him on the way out: the one seated on the throne was the King of Hades, surname Pak, given name Oo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The King of Yom-na (Hell)' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Hong's Tour of the Hells of Yom-na

texts.period: Story of Hong Nai-pom (1561-1644); his death-vision dated 1594; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Hong's Experiences in Hades', eBook #51002

summary.en: Hong Nai-pom of Pyongyang dies of typhus in 1594 and is laid in his coffin; the body turns and falls with a thud, and he lives again. In the dream he stood among ogres with bulls' heads while a black-robed scribe condemned the blasphemer of the Buddha to ten thousand kalpas in hell — until a golden-faced Buddha smiled and corrected the record: this man must live to eighty-three and attain the Second Degree. Given a tour, Hong sees the prison of Stirrers-up of Strife with its pit of fire and red-hot rods, the hell of Liars where tongues are chained to an iron pillar, the hell of Deceivers where ogres cut flesh from corrupt officials and metal snakes and copper dogs suck their blood — and at last the Home of the Blessed, haloed in clouds of glory, where hundreds of priests keep the faith. He wakes dead four days; his age and rank come about exactly as the Buddha predicted, and he never stops telling what he saw.
summary.zh: 洪乃範平壤人，甲午（1594）患傷寒卒，斂於棺。屍忽自仆，家人驚救，遂甦。自言夢入冥府，牛首鬼卒圍之；皂衣吏斥其謗佛，當墮地獄萬劫。忽有金面如來含笑曰：『此人壽當八十三，官至二品。』乃導之遍觀諸獄：撥弄是非獄有火坑烙目，妄語獄以鐵鏈懸舌，偽善貪官獄有銅犬鐵蛇噬血——最後至極樂之鄉，僧眾持戒者蓮花繞身。醒後述其所見，其壽其官果如佛言。

sensitivity.note: Korean vision-of-hell literature (chiemon genre); graphic torments paraphrased at summary level.

passages.text: Hong Nai-pom was a military graduate of Pyeng-yang. In 1594 he fell ill of typhus fever, and after ten days of suffering died; his body was prepared for burial and placed in a coffin. Of a sudden the body turned itself and fell with a thud to the ground; from this time on the body resumed its functions, and Hong lived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Hong's Experiences in Hades' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: In his dream he went to a place of great fear where many persons stood around, and awful ogres, some wearing bulls' heads, crowded about him. A scribe robed in black sat on a platform: 'You have ever been a blasphemer of the Buddha, and a denier of a future life. You are now to be sent to hell, and ten thousand kalpas will not see you out of it.' Just at that moment a certain Buddha with a face of shining gold came smiling toward him: 'There is truly a mistake somewhere; this man must attain to the age of eighty-three and become an officer of the Second Degree ere he dies. Now that you have come, look about the place before you go, and tell the world afterwards of what you have seen.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Hong's Experiences in Hades' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: He was brought first to the prison-house marked Stirrers-up of Strife, with a great brazier-shaped pit of stones filled with fire, where the guilty were made to sit close before it and an infernal guard took a long red-hot rod of iron and put out their eyes. The next hell was marked Liars: an iron pillar several yards high, the offenders kneeling before it with knives driven through their tongues and iron chains through each, hanging them dangled by the tongues, stones tied to their feet. The next was marked Deceivers: there ogres cut the flesh from the bodies of corrupt officeholders and fed it to starving demons, while metal snakes and copper dogs crowded in to bite them and suck their blood. 'When these offenders were on earth they held high office, pretended to be true and good, received bribes in secret, ate the fat of the land and sucked the blood of the people, and yet advertised themselves as benefactors.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Hong's Experiences in Hades' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the guides took him south-east to a great house marked The Home of the Blessed, beautiful haloes encircling it and clouds of glory, where hundreds of priests in cassock and surplice sat, some with fresh-blown lotus flowers, some like the Buddha. 'These when on earth kept the faith, and with undivided hearts served the Buddha, and so have escaped the Eight Sorrows and the Ten Punishments.' While on the way back he awakened with a start and found that he had been dead for four days. His age and Second Degree of rank came about just as the Buddha had predicted; Im Bang records it, saying, don't find fault with the story, but learn its lesson.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Hong's Experiences in Hades' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Haunted Houses of Ink Town

region.en: Ink Town and South Ward, Seoul (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Told as personal experience by Yi Chang of Seoul; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Haunted Houses', eBook #51002

summary.en: Poor and homeless, Yi Chang takes haunted houses in Seoul to live in. In Ink Town a locked upper room holds a tablet chair, a stringless old harp, worn shoes and sticks under years of dust; at midnight harp music and a great unintelligible carousing fill the house, and a sword-thrust through the partition is answered by a sharp blue blade thrust out from the other side. In the South Ward two dogs with fiery red eyes lie unmoving on the verandah until midnight, when they bay at the inky sky as a man in ceremonial robes arrives, greeted with delight by the dogs, before whom five or six multi-coloured demons bow; he leads dogs and demons round the house, and all vanish — the devils into a hole under the floor, found next day to contain only an old sieve and discarded brooms. Others who try the houses fare no better: a servant dies before the burning of the harp is finished, and a woman in a blue skirt comes down from a loft.
summary.zh: 李昌貧而僦居凶宅。墨坊一宅上有鎖閉之樓，中有神主椅、無絃舊琴、敝履朽木。夜半聞樂聲與喧鬧聲，破壁窺之，壁中忽出青鋒，遂不敢近。南洞一宅有二犬，目赤如火，晝伏不動；夜半向天狂吠，有衣冠者至，群妖羅拜，隨之行宅一周而俱滅——明日驗地板下，惟舊篩敝帚而已。又有舉子焚琴者，火未竟而一僕暴斃，遂止。

passages.text: There once lived a man in Seoul called Yi Chang, who was poor and had no home of his own, so he lived much in quarters loaned him by others; when hard pressed he even went into haunted houses. One such house in Ink Town at the foot of South Mountain had been haunted for generations and was left vacant. It had one upper room fast locked, wherein through a chink were seen a tablet chair and stand, an old harp without strings, a pair of worn shoes, some sticks and bits of wood, the dust lying thick as though gathered through long years of time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Haunted Houses' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The company, after drinking wine, watched the night through. Towards midnight they suddenly heard the sound of harps and a great multitude of voices, as though many people were gathered and carousing at a feast. One drew a sword and struck a hole through the partition that looked into the tower; instantly there appeared from the other side a sharp blade thrust out toward them, blue in colour. In fear and consternation they desisted; but the sound of the harp and the revelry kept up till the morning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Haunted Houses' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the South Ward there was another haunted house. On entering, they found two dogs within the enclosure, one black and one tan, lying on the open verandah, their eyes fiery red, neither barking nor biting. When midnight came the two animals got down into the court and began baying at the inky sky. Then some one came round the corner of the house dressed in ceremonial robes; the two dogs met him with great delight, jumping up before and behind in their joy at his coming. Five or six multi-coloured demons appeared and bowed before him; the man led the demons and the dogs two or three times round the house, till at last all of them mysteriously disappeared — the devils into a hole underneath the floor, the dogs up to their quarters to lie down. When daylight came they examined under the floor and saw only an old, worn-out sieve and a few discarded brooms.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Haunted Houses' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: There was still another tale of a graduate who went into a haunted dwelling in Ink Town and had the old harp, the spirit chair, the shoes and sticks burned; before the fire had finished its work, one of the servants fell down and died, and the graduate in fear put out the fire, restored the things and left the house. Again, another homeless man saw in the night a woman in a blue skirt come down from the loft, acting in a peculiar and uncanny way, and left with his belongings. In South Kettle Town woodmen passing behind a haunted house found an old woman sitting weeping under a tree; thinking her an evil bogey, one man came up behind and gave her a thrust with his sickle, and the witch rushed off into the house, her height appearing to be only about one cubit and a span.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Haunted Houses' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: General Im and the Duel over the Lake

region.zh: 白頭山支脈太白山（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of the youth of General Im Kyong-up (d. 1628), later worshipped in many parts of Korea; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Im, the Hunter', eBook #51002

summary.en: Young Im Kyong-up, hunting deer on foot in the Wol-lak Mountains, is overtaken by night on Tai-paik Mountain and directed by a woodman to a great tiled mansion standing alone. The woodman feeds him, then takes up a great sword: 'To-night there is something on hand worth the seeing.' Through endless gates they come to a lake where lights shine from a pavilion; the woodman leaps the water, and from a tree Im watches two figures vault into mid-air, steel clashing and fire flashing for a long time — then a thud and a cry of victory in the woodman's voice. The vanquished was his wife's lover, a 'great and gifted man' who humbly sold cut tobacco inside the South Gate of Seoul. The woodman weeps at killing him, offers Im the house and the woman, and when Im refuses, strikes off her head; then he teaches the young man the use of the sword for six days. Im's bones grow cold even in the telling; the Fates, the woodman says, have decided he will fail half-way.
summary.zh: 林業俊少獵太白山中，迷路遇樵者，引至孤宅。夜半偕至湖亭，登樹觀之：樵者躍湖而入，與一人決鬥於空中，刀光火影，久而一人墮地。樵者勝而泣曰：『所殺者，賣煙草之異人也，大器而屈於下僚。』乃贈屋與婦，林辭；樵者遂斬婦，留林六日授劍術，且言其命當中道而止。後林果為名將而卒困於時。

sensitivity.note: Tale about a general later worshipped as a shamanic war god; depicts a killing but at summary level.

passages.text: When General Im Kyong-up was young he lived in the town of Tallai and loved the chase. Once, tracking deer on foot as far as Tai-paik Mountain, he was overtaken by night, with yawning chasms and great cliffs on all sides. A woodman directed him to a cliff opposite where there was a house: a great tiled mansion standing alone, quiet, dark, and vacant. Some one opened the room door and shouted, 'Do you sleep here? Have you had something to eat?' — the same person that had directed him on his way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Im, the Hunter' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The woodman opened the wall box and brought out wine and meat; then took from it a great sword. Im asked, 'What is this you have; do you intend to kill me?' The woodman laughed, 'No, no, but to-night there is something on hand worth the seeing. Will you come with me and not be afraid?' About midnight they went through a succession of gates to a place where lights were reflected on a pond, with a high pavilion in the middle of the lake and sounds of laughter from the upper storey. The woodman told Im to climb a large tree near the right pavilion, tie himself fast to the trunk and keep perfectly still.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Im, the Hunter' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: From his vantage Im saw the woodman give a leap that cleared the lake and landed him in the pavilion; then the woodman and his neighbour arose, came to the entrance, and vaulted off into mid-air, where they disappeared from sight — nothing to be distinguished but the clashing of steel and flashes of fire for a long time. Then something fell to the ground with a great thud, and a cry of victory arose that he recognized as the woodman's voice. Chills ran all over him and goose-flesh covered his skin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Im, the Hunter' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The woodman said, 'I am not an ordinary mortal of the world, but an outlaw of the hills and woods; by robbing I have many such houses, a beautiful woman in each. All unexpectedly this woman has neglected me for another man. There were mighty possibilities in him, though he lived humbly inside the South Gate of Seoul and sold cut tobacco. Alas, I have killed a great and gifted man. You have courage, but it is not sufficient to meet a world like this; you will fail half-way, the Fates have so decided. Cease from any vain ambitions, and take over this woman and this home.' Im shook his head; the woodman said, 'If you do not, there is nothing for this woman but death,' and struck her with his sword and cut off her head. The day following he said, 'Since you are determined to go forth and do valiantly, stay with me a little and learn the use of the sword.' Im stayed for six days and learned it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Im, the Hunter' (1913); not verbatim.

texts.period: Collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Magic Invasion of Seoul', eBook #51002

summary.en: Crossing the Han River, a gentleman of Seoul dreams of a majestic red-bearded rider on a red horse who dashes a pen-mark on his hand as the sign of the God of War: seven horses loaded with network hampers will come from the far South; show them the sign and they will kill themselves; burn the loads, but don't look into them. Waking, the mark is there, the ink not yet dry. On the bank he shows it; the official-coated leader leaps over the cliff into the river and his eight or nine men follow. The Board of War burns the hampers in Seoul, and from the fire come tumbling little figures of men and horses, an inch long, in countless numbers — the creation of a magician, intended for a monster invasion of Seoul until warned by Kwan. From that time the people of Seoul began faithful offerings to the God of War, for had he not saved the city?
summary.zh: 漢江舟中，一士晝寐，夢見絳面長髯將軍乘赤馬，於其掌心以筆畫符曰：『此關帝之符也。南來七騎負網籃者，乃妖術害京之具，出符示之，彼自盡；積薪焚之，毋啟視。』醒而符尚濕。江干果遇七騎，示符，為首者躍崖投江，從者皆隨之。兵曹焚其籃於京中，火發處湧出人馬小偶，寸許長，不可勝數——術士所造，欲以妖法陷都城者也。都人自是崇祀關帝，以其救城之功。

sensitivity.note: Kwan (Guan Yu) war-god cult tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: A gentleman of Seoul was one day crossing the Han River in a boat. In the crossing he nodded for a moment and dreamed a dream: he met a man with Gothic eyebrows and almond eyes, whose face was red as ripened dates, dressed in green with a long beard, a man of majestic appearance with a great sword at his side, riding on a red horse. He asked the gentleman to open his hand, and dashed a pen-mark on it as the sign of the God of War.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Magic Invasion of Seoul' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'When you cross the river, do not go direct to Seoul, but wait at the landing. Seven horses will shortly appear, loaded with network hampers, all proceeding on their journey to the capital. You are to call the horsemen, open your hand, and show them the sign. When they see it they will all commit suicide in your very presence. After that, take the loads and pile them up, but don't look into them. Then go at once and report the matter to the Palace and have them all burned.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Magic Invasion of Seoul' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The gentleman gave a great start of terror and awoke. He looked at his hand, and there, indeed, was the strange mark, the ink not yet dried upon it. He waited on the river's bank; in a little there came the seven loads on seven horses from the far-distant South, attendants in charge and one man wearing an official coat. When he showed them the sign, the man in the official coat turned and with one bound jumped over the cliff into the river, and the eight or nine who accompanied the loads all rushed after him and dashed into the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Magic Invasion of Seoul' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Board of War had the loads brought into Seoul, piled high with wood and set on fire. When the fire developed, the baskets broke open, and little figures of men and horses, each an inch or so long, in countless numbers, came tumbling out; the officials were frozen with fear until the hampers were all burned up. These were the creation of a magician, and were intended for a monster invasion of Seoul, until warned by Kwan. From that time on the people of Seoul began faithful offerings to the God of War, for had he not saved the city?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Magic Invasion of Seoul' (1913); not verbatim.
